newsitem.title: USA: Venezuelan bankers ordered to pay over $8 million.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan bankers ordered to pay over $8 million.

text.p: Manhattan Supreme Court Judge Edward McLaughlin on Tuesday ordered a Latin American banker and his son to pay more than $8 million in restitution to depositors in their failed bank.
Orlando Castro Llanes, 71, and his son, Orlando Castro Castro, 47, were also fined $100,000 each. No date has been set in the sentencing of Jorge Castro Barredo, 29, a grandson also found guilty.

The restitution order comes after last month's sentencing of the two to prison. The judge also said that if the two defendants, convicted of fraud and grand larceny, failed to come up with the $8.4 million in restitution, an additional one year in prison would be tacked on to their sentences.
The judge sentenced Castro Llanes last month to at least one year in jail but no more than three years. His son was given a 2 1/3 to seven-year prison sentence for playing a key role in the scandal.

Prosecutors said the three defendants illegally used deposits in a family controlled bank, Banco Progreso International de Puerto Rico (BPIPR) to prop up financial institutions they controlled in Central and South America.
The Castro Llanes business empire in Venezuela included banks, four insurance firms, 40 radio stations, car rental companies and coffee manufacturing plants.

Richard Sharpstein, the lawyer for Castro Llanes told the judge his client is bankrupt. The lawyer also said there was an "on-going process of liquidation" going on in Puerto Rico and that all depositors would ultimately get their money.
The prosecution said the three men misled Venezuelan depositors to believe their bank was a safe offshore bank subject to tight regulatory control, attracting deposits of more than $55 million.
Their bank in Puerto Rico closed in January 1995 with uninsured losses to depositors of more than $15 million.
Prosecutors also claimed the defendants lied to regulators in Puerto Rico by falsely claiming bank funds were held in Panama and thus not subject to Puerto Rican oversight.
The case was tried in New York because prosecutors said money in the alleged fraud was transferred through New York banks.
Defense lawyers have filed a notice of appeal. Sharpstein said a key issue in the appeal was whether New York had jurisdiction.
